channel.description: Recent content in Engineering Fieldnotes on Trayson Rubio

item.title: Faster sweeps, better questions for each hit
item.description:
The serial scan was doing a lot of retuning just to ask whether anything was there. Broad/Fast now groups the 2,652 configured channel centers into 97 wide windows, checks each for about 0.128 seconds, and extracts up to the three strongest channels when a window crosses threshold. On paper that’s about 12.4 seconds of probe time for a pass, before USB/FFT work, tuner settling, and the five-second triggered dwells.

It makes the survey much quicker, with a tradeoff: a brief burst can fall between probes, and only the strongest few channels in a busy window make it to full capture. This is a way to find leads, not continuous coverage.

item.title: A checksum turned a pulse pattern into real frames
item.description:
I went back to the original, unfiltered 60-second capture centered at 433.900 MHz. Two signals sat near 433.8885 and 433.9114 MHz. The first promising decode was mis-sliced; I had to stop trusting the bit string and look for structure that repeated.

The revised parser found a D3 91 sync word, read the following length field, and checked a CRC-16 before accepting a frame. It recovered 396 CRC-valid frames and rejected 67 apparent syncs that failed the check. The frames fall into two recurring groups: 84 short frames with payload 00, and 312 frames with payload 11 22 33. Both include the same sync and valid length/check fields.

item.title: Turn one-off scripts into a review console
item.description:
Once the overnight scan started producing hundreds of candidates, I needed a place to review them without losing the trail. I built a small PySide desktop app with separate Basic Scan, Broad/Fast Scan, and Digital Scan modes, dated run folders, profiles, capture playback, and a shared encounter log.

The first classifier pass was deliberately a screen, not a verdict. Replaying the 2026-10-11 run with version 2.0 left 533 noise, 198 review, and 1 voice candidate. I kept the review bucket wide because weak audio and unknown modulation are easy to mislabel. A person can mark voice/no voice after listening; those labels are saved for future analysis, but they do not train the current classifier.

item.title: Known weather packets, then an unknown one
item.description:
At 433.94 MHz, rtl_433 gave me a nice sanity check: it recognized repeating Oregon weather-sensor packets and produced structured readings. That confirmed the capture-and-decode path was working for at least one known format.

Then a targeted capture around 433.9125 MHz produced a pulse train that the built-in decoders didn’t recognize. I generated a local report with the pulse timing and signal plots, and started treating it as an unknown packet format instead of calling it a device. My first bit slicing was wrong; what looked like a short frame was a parsing artifact. Keeping the capture made it possible to revisit the same RF data as the parser improved.

item.title: Keep the I/Q; audio can wait
item.description:
Saving only demodulated audio was a dead end for digital signals. I switched the hit recorder to keep raw complex samples alongside the NFM WAV, so I could come back later and try another filter or decoder without needing the radio to hear the transmission again.

That exposed a couple of practical wrinkles. The scan notices a signal before it starts the five-second capture, so a short transmission can be mostly gone by then. And for NFM, filtering the channel before FM demodulation made a much cleaner result than trying to demodulate the whole 1.024 MHz capture first. A nearby DMR repeater also explained why a strong hit could sound like hash on the analog audio path: strong RF isn’t the same thing as analog voice.

item.title: First sweep: make the radio do the boring part
item.description:
The first version was a Python loop around the RTL-SDR: tune a channel, take a short look, and save a capture when the signal crossed a threshold. The goal was simple—cover the local VHF/UHF channels without sitting there retuning by hand.

The first broad grid had 5,601 channels. At a quarter second per probe, one pass could take roughly 23 minutes before tuner settling or file work. That was too slow for casual experiments, so I added focused profiles for the bands and frequencies I actually wanted to watch. A plotted sweep also made one strong, repeatable feature around 445.0375 MHz stand out. That was a useful lead, but a peak alone doesn’t tell me what modulation or user is behind it.

item.title: Make the packet work in software before blaming the air
item.description:
The Pi side now has a small, testable path for building and checking packets: a packet model, CRC, Manchester codec, and a frame parser that searches for preamble/sync before validating length and checksum. The conversation’s Pi session reported 63 pytest checks passing. That’s encouraging for the software protocol path; it says nothing yet about receiver timing over the radio.

One useful design boundary is still visible in the code: GPIO timing is an interface, not a finished pigpio implementation. The current command-line tool decodes logical packet bytes offline. The PIC folder in this repository is still a handoff/readme, so I’m not counting firmware behavior as demonstrated here.

item.title: The wiring question was part of the protocol work
item.description:
When the modules came out on the bench, the receiver’s 5V marking raised the important question: what voltage is actually coming back out of DATA? The Pi’s GPIO is 3.3 V. Feeding the module from 5 V does not make a 5 V DATA output safe for a Pi pin.

The sensible next step is to measure the receiver output and use a level shifter or divider if it exceeds the Pi’s input limit. The conversation stopped before that was verified, and I don’t see a captured packet or concrete GPIO receiver in this repo. So the honest status is: protocol and offline software are in place; the first over-the-air receive is still ahead.

item.title: Write the packet contract before either side drifts
item.description:
I set up one repository for both processors: a shared protocol document at the root, a Raspberry Pi implementation, and a PIC handoff area. That gives the two sides one place to agree on bytes and timing while leaving timer and GPIO details with the firmware they belong to.

Protocol v1 uses ASK/OOK at a nominal 2,000 bits per second. Each logical bit becomes a Manchester pair (0 → 01, 1 → 10), preceded by eight 0x55 bytes and sync D3 91. The packet carries version, type, source, destination, sequence, payload length, up to 32 payload bytes, then CRC-16-CCITT. That is enough structure to reject noise and malformed frames without making the first firmware pass huge.

item.title: First question: how much of the radio should I build myself?
item.description:
The idea was to get a PIC and a Raspberry Pi talking over a pair of inexpensive FS1000A 433 MHz modules. I wanted to learn the whole path, but didn’t want to invent a protocol just for the sake of it. The useful split was to borrow the familiar pieces—preamble, sync, balanced coding, length, checksum—and define a small shared contract both ends could implement.

The first proof is intentionally one way: make the PIC send a known DATA packet and have the Pi receive and validate it. If that behaves, add acknowledgements and retries. Keeping the first milestone narrow gives us a clean place to debug before adding a round trip.

item.title: Outdoor enclosure and first field readings
item.description:
I printed a vented enclosure with a downward-facing sensor opening and a separate sealed electronics compartment. The sensor sits behind a replaceable membrane to reduce splash exposure.

The first outdoor test ran for three days. The logger stayed online, though direct afternoon sun warmed the sensor by about 2 ?C. I?ll add a small radiation shield before treating the temperature data as representative.

Reference: Sensor datasheet

item.title: First prototype and power budget
item.description:
The first bench prototype uses a small microcontroller board, a digital temperature and humidity sensor, and a light sensor. The immediate goal is to measure sleep current before choosing a battery and panel.

Initial power estimate

Mode Current Duration per hour
Deep sleep 22 ?A 58 min
Sensor sample 8 mA 2 s
Radio upload 42 mA 3 s

The radio dominates the short active window. Next I?ll verify the real average with a current profiler and check the sensor readings against a reference thermometer.
